Sources: inbound.rs: how a wire frame becomes the leg’s call (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/rust/crates/fantastic-io-bridge/src/inbound.rs#L1); ws.rs: the WebSocket frames (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/rust/crates/bundles/fantastic-web/src/ws.rs#L1); web_ws readme (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/rust/crates/bundles/fantastic-web-ws/src/readme.md); web_rest readme (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/rust/crates/bundles/fantastic-web-rest/src/readme.md); the bridge crate: forward and the frame protocol (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/rust/crates/bundles/fantastic-bridge/src/lib.rs#L1); peers.rs: <guid>|<agent> addressing (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/rust/crates/fantastic-kernel/src/peers.rs#L1); fantastic mcp (the MCP server face) (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/docs/mcp.md); mcp_client (a remote server’s tools as verbs) (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/rust/crates/bundles/fantastic-mcp-client/src/lib.rs#L1)

### Foundations › Protocol › The contract

URL: https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/protocol/contract/

Fantastic has two host runtimes, Python and Rust, and a TypeScript kernel for the browser. A caller must get the same answer from any of them. Writing that down as a test in each language would let the tests drift apart.

The repository instead states each wire-visible property once, as data, in the `contract/` folder. Each runtime has a small driver that replays the data against its own kernel. This page shows what is in the folder, how the drivers hold a reply to a case, and where the runtimes are allowed to differ.

#### What is in contract/

The folder holds the **contract**: what the substrate claims, as files that no runtime owns. Every runtime reads them with the tools it already has, so the TypeScript kernel needs no extra dependencies and the cases are JSON.

| file | what it pins |
|---|---|
| `requirements.yaml` | the registry of requirement ids, such as `TSG-1`, and whether a failure of each is a `MUST` |
| `conformance/cases.json` | 9 cases: one envelope, answered the same by every runtime and transport |
| `memory_store/cases.json` | 15 scenarios that every memory store (`ram_store`, `sqlite_store`) must answer the same |
| `home/v1/cases.json` | the `home` protocol, version 1: replayed by the Rust agent and the TypeScript client |
| `agentic/configs`, `agentic/specs` | deployable kernel shapes, and ordered steps that each must prove |

Python is the reference. The contributing guide says that when implementations disagree, Python is right, and that a protocol change in only one host is a bug.

#### A case is a send and what the reply must hold

A case in `conformance/cases.json` has a `name`, a `target`, a `payload`, and what to check. `expect` lists keys and values that must appear in the reply. `expect_keys` lists keys that must exist. Extra keys in the reply are allowed, so a case names only what it means to pin.

one case, as written in cases.json:

```
{"name": "custom-verb", "target": "c21_probe",
 "payload": {"type": "poke", "value": 41},
 "expect": {"poked": 41}}
```

Each driver builds the same small fixture: an agent `c21_probe` that answers `poke` with `{poked: value}`, and an id `c21_nobody` that never exists. The cases then reach past the happy path. Sending `reflect` to `c21_nobody` must answer `reason: unknown_agent`. An empty payload must answer `missing_arg` with `arg: payload.type`. A kernel verb such as `ps` sent to a non-root agent must answer `not_here` and name the verb.

*Animation: One file of cases, every runtime* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/protocol/contract/replay.mp4). A case from cases.json is shown: send {"type": "poke", "value": 41}, expect {"poked": 41}. Python, Rust and TS each send it to their own kernel, and each reply holds {"poked": 41}. A second case sends reflect to c21_nobody and expects reason unknown_agent, and all three answer it.

The checks use `reason`, the machine field of every [refusal](/fantastic/foundations/protocol/refusals/), not the prose of `error`. So two runtimes may word an error differently and still pass.

Cases replay in order against one kernel, so a case that changes state must come first and be repeatable. The tree-changing verbs `create_agent`, `update_agent` and `delete_agent` are not in this file. Their answer depends on who sends, so each runtime pins them in its own tests and in the agentic specs.

#### Three drivers, one file

Adding a case to the file puts every runtime on the hook for it. There is no per-runtime test to forget. The drivers are short.

- **Rust** reads the file, sends each case through the kernel in order, and asserts that every case was checked.
- **Python** replays it too, and adds the transport legs described below.
- **TypeScript** runs one test per case, each on a fresh kernel.

All three hold the reply to the same rule: every key in `expect` must be in the reply with an equal value, and every key in `expect_keys` must exist. No test compares a Rust reply with a Python reply directly. Both are held to the same written answer, which is what makes the data the contract.

#### Python also diffs the transports

The Python driver sends the same cases down five **legs** of one kernel: in-process, a websocket bridge, a REST route, an `exec` guest and a relay tunnel. It turns every reply into JSON with sorted keys, so a wire reply and an in-process object compare on equal terms. Each leg’s reply must equal the in-process reply.

*Animation: Five transports, one answer* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/protocol/contract/legs.mp4). Python sends the poke case on five legs: in-proc, ws-bridge, web-rest, exec-guest and relay-tunnel. Each reply equals the in-proc reference. For the ledger case, marked pairwise: false, the legs are checked for shape only, because ledger is scoped to the sender.

Attribution differs by design. In-process the sender is the operator, and each other leg dispatches as its own agent. So the fixture grants every leg the same reach on both halves of the [call gate](/fantastic/foundations/protocol/call-gate/), and the cases avoid testing the gate itself. What must be identical is the reply.

Two cases are marked `pairwise: false`: `reflect` on the kernel and `ledger`. They are checked for shape on every leg but not compared across legs. The root’s live state differs between legs’ runs, and `ledger` is scoped to the sender that made the calls, so each leg sees its own executions.

#### Where runtimes may differ, in writing

Two things are allowed to differ, and both are written down. The first is the root id. A case writes `$root`, and each driver replaces it with its own root id before it compares. All three drivers use `kernel_state`. The placeholder keeps the rule “each runtime’s own value, never equality” in the data, and it would allow a different root id. None of the three differs today.

contract/README.md says the Rust root is `core`. The Rust driver and its `DEFAULT_ROOT_ID` say `kernel_state`, and the code wins.

The second is a verb a runtime does not own. The browser kernel does not own the tree verbs (`create_agent`, `update_agent`, `list_agents`), so its driver skips the `list_agents` case by name and records the reason in the driver. Anything not named must pass. A skip is a visible, reviewed line, not a quiet gap.

*Animation: Differences are named* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/protocol/contract/named.mp4). The reflect-kernel case expects {"id": "$root"}. Each runtime swaps in its own root id, kernel_state, and passes. For list-agents-limited, Python and Rust pass and the TS driver skips the case by name, with its reason recorded in the driver.

#### Steps with a cause: the agentic corpus

A flat table can state a verdict but not a cause. The agentic corpus pairs a **config**, a kernel shape you could deploy, with a **spec**, an ordered list of steps that says what must be true of it. A config holds no test data and a spec holds no system data, and both are parsed strictly: an unknown key is an error naming its file.

The steps use a few verbs. `reach` sends as an agent through the gate, and `operator` sends with operator authority. `grant` and `revoke` change one half of an edge, `reboot` persists and rehydrates, and `reconcile_grants` and `sweep_undeclared` walk what the manifest declares rather than a hand-written list.

Order is the point. The `two_sided_gate` spec opens one half of an edge at a time. With neither half the send is refused at `egress`. With only the sender’s half the refusal moves to `ingress`. Only with both does it pass. That move proves the second half was refusing on its own all along.

Every step can carry `because: <requirement-id>`, and a spec may not claim a requirement that no step tags. The Python and Rust runners run this corpus. The TypeScript kernel does not, because it has no manifest loader to hydrate a declared roster. Its own tests cover the gate, the ledger, batch send, refusals and paging.

#### How Rust and Python stay twins

Three habits keep the two host runtimes close. Python is the reference, and a Rust module says when it is a port. The Rust refusal module is a “Port of python `kernel/_refusal.py` (canonical)”, and it documents that its key order matches Python’s.

A protocol change lands in both hosts, and the shared corpus fails if one is missed. The memory stores show the same habit at smaller scale: in both runtimes the RAM store and the SQLite store replay the same 15 scenarios, and their transcripts must match, apart from the error prose of an unhandled reply and the text of `reflect`, so a caller cannot tell the stores apart.

The corpus does not make the runtimes identical. It makes the claims that matter checkable from outside: the same envelope, the same reply, and each difference named in the data or in a driver.

Sources: contract/README.md: the corpus and the steps DSL (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/contract/README.md#L1); conformance/cases.json: the 9 shared cases (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/contract/conformance/cases.json#L6); Python driver: five transport legs (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/python/tests/conformance/test_c21_transport_symmetry.py#L365); Rust driver: c21_conformance.rs (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/rust/crates/fantastic-kernel/tests/c21_conformance.rs#L124); TypeScript driver: skips by name (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/ts/tests/c21_conformance.test.ts#L44); agentic spec: the two-sided gate ladder (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/contract/agentic/specs/two_sided_gate.yaml#L1); memory_store/cases.json: one answer from every store (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/contract/memory_store/cases.json#L2); CONTRIBUTING.md: cross-runtime parity (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md#L33)

### Foundations › Kernel

URL: https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/kernel/

The thesis names a “mediator that handles the communication exchange.” The kernel is that mediator: it holds the agents, routes every send between them and keeps track of the work in flight.

#### What the kernel holds

Every agent is a **record** in one tree: an `id`, a `handler_module` that names its **bundle** (the code that answers its verbs) and a `parent_id`. The tree says who owns whom; a send finds its target in one flat map from id to agent. [Agents as records](/fantastic/foundations/kernel/records/) covers the record, the tree and `reflect`.

A set of fourteen verbs belongs to the kernel itself and only the root answers them, such as `create_agent`, `update_agent`, `delete_agent`, `ps` and `cancel`. The agent you name is the operand, not the actor: sending one of these verbs to any other agent gets a `not_here` refusal that names the fix. [Lifecycle](/fantastic/foundations/kernel/lifecycle/) follows an agent from `create_agent` to `delete_agent`, and the kernel from `kernel_start` to `kernel_stop`.

Every item of a send that reaches its target runs as a kernel task. The task table works like Unix: `ps` lists what is in flight, `cancel` stops a task and its subtree, and `await_set` wakes a lead once for a set of reports ([Tasks and waiting](/fantastic/foundations/kernel/tasks/)).

*Animation: One send, a batch of calls* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/protocol/messages/batch.mp4). A model turn sends three items in one batch. The kernel registers all three as tasks in ps before any reply; they run concurrently and finish in any order, and the reply array keeps the input order: one {pid, status, result} per item.

There are two host kernels, Rust and Python, and they answer the same verbs. The Rust kernel’s files describe themselves as rule-for-rule ports of the Python kernel, “which is canonical.” The main difference is how bundles load: Rust crates implement a `Bundle` trait, Python finds handler modules through entry points, and both load folder bundles ([Bundles and twin runtimes](/fantastic/foundations/kernel/bundles/)).

What survives a restart depends on two agents you wire: a `file_bridge` rooted at `.fantastic` keeps the tree on disk, and a durable memory store keeps the kernel’s execution rows. One counter names every call, task and row ([State and durability](/fantastic/foundations/kernel/state/)).

In this part: Agents as records (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/kernel/records/); Lifecycle (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/kernel/lifecycle/); Bundles and twin runtimes (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/kernel/bundles/); Tasks and waiting (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/kernel/tasks/); State and durability (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/kernel/state/)

Sources: THESIS.md (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/THESIS.md#L5); README.md: agents and send (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/README.md#L42); README.md: kernel services (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/README.md#L63); system-verbs.md (the kernel verbs) (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/rust/crates/bundles/fantastic-core/src/docs/system-verbs.md#L5); rows.rs: a port of the Python kernel (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/rust/crates/fantastic-kernel/src/rows.rs#L4); persistence.rs: the tree on disk, through a file_bridge (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/rust/crates/fantastic-kernel/src/persistence.rs#L163); bundle.rs: the Bundle trait (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/rust/crates/fantastic-kernel/src/bundle.rs#L50); _bundles.py: entry points (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/python/kernel/_bundles.py#L1)

### Foundations › Kernel › Agents as records

URL: https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/kernel/records/

In Fantastic a model, a program, a shell and the human at the keyboard are all agents in one tree, reached the same way. The kernel knows an agent by one small thing: its record.

This page shows what a record holds, how the records form one tree, and how the `reflect` verb reads that tree back without flooding a caller with text.

#### The record

An agent is a **record** plus the **bundle** that answers its verbs. The record has an `id`, unique across the whole tree, and a `handler_module` that names the bundle. Every other field sits flat at the top level of the record. A `parent_id` says who owns the agent; the root has none.

Those flat fields are how a bundle is configured: a `display_name`, a `description`, a port, a root folder. The code calls them the record’s **meta**, but it does not nest them under a `meta` key. In the Rust kernel the record is a struct with `id`, `handler_module`, `parent_id` and a map for everything else.

a record (illustrative id):

```
id              file_bridge_3f9a1c
handler_module  file_bridge.tools
display_name    files
can_call        {"$self": "*"}
callable_by     {"$self": "*"}
parent_id       kernel_state
```

The key order is part of the record. Both runtimes write `id`, `handler_module`, the other fields and then `parent_id`. The parent comes last because the tree decides where an agent sits: a `parent_id` that leaked into the flat fields must not shadow it.

*Animation: An agent is a record* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/kernel/records/record.mp4). create_agent names the bundle file_bridge.tools and the owner kernel_state, and sends no id. The kernel mints file_bridge_3f9a1c, copies display_name from the payload, stamps can_call and callable_by, and writes parent_id last.

#### Where a record comes from

The kernel verb `create_agent` makes a record. It requires a `handler_module` and a `parent_id`. Placement is stated, never inferred from who sent the call: `parent_id` names the owner, which can be the caller’s own id or `kernel_state` for a top-level agent. The reserved address `kernel` stands for the root here too.

create_agent (illustrative values):

```
[{"target": "kernel", "payload": {"type": "create_agent",
  "handler_module": "file_bridge.tools",
  "parent_id": "kernel_state", "display_name": "files"}}]
```

Every field in the payload except `type`, `id`, `handler_module` and `parent_id` becomes a flat field of the record. If the payload has no `id`, the kernel mints one as `<bundle>_<hex6>`: the second-last dotted segment of the handler module, then six random hex digits. `file_bridge.tools` gives `file_bridge_3f9a1c`. An id that is already taken is refused with `exists`. An id becomes a folder name, so it must be one safe path segment.

A write is judged before it lands. The names `root_path`, `ctx` and `parent` are reserved for the kernel’s own wiring, and a record may not carry them. The shape of `can_call` and `callable_by` is checked, and the bundle may add its own `validate_meta` check. A refused write comes back as a refusal in the [common shape](/fantastic/foundations/protocol/refusals/), with a `reason` such as `bad_arg` or `invalid_meta`.

The `handler_module` is fixed once the agent exists: `update_agent` refuses it. Two fields are stamped on every record when the kernel builds the agent: `can_call` and `callable_by`, each starting as `{"$self": "*"}`, merged under any grant the record already carries. They are the two halves of the [call gate](/fantastic/foundations/protocol/call-gate/).

Comments in the Rust and Python kernels still describe the starting grants as `$self`, `$parent` and `$subtree`. The constants in both runtimes hold `{"$self": "*"}` only, and this page follows the constants.

#### One tree

Every agent has exactly one parent. The root has the id `kernel_state` and no parent, and every other agent sits below it. An agent’s children keep their creation order.

The tree does not carry messages. The kernel keeps one flat map from id to agent, which the Rust kernel calls its only routing table. A send looks its target id up in that map and does not walk from parent to child.

The tree answers a different question: who owns what. It decides what `delete_agent` takes with it, because a delete cascades depth first through the subtree. It decides what the `$parent` and `$subtree` keys of a grant mean, because `$subtree` is every agent below the holder. And it decides what `reflect` shows. The root cannot be deleted.

*Animation: One tree, one flat map* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/kernel/records/tree.mp4). Five agents sit in one tree under kernel_state. The kernel also keeps a flat map from id to agent. A send from writer to files is resolved in that map, not by walking the tree. The tree shows ownership: team’s subtree is team, writer and reviewer.

On disk the tree mirrors the ownership. Each agent is an `agent.yaml` in its own folder, and its children are folders below it, in a container named by the root record’s `children_dir` field, `agents` by default, the same for every agent in the tree. The tree lives in `.fantastic/` of the folder the kernel runs in. The `kernel_state` root writes the records, not `create_agent` itself, and only through a `file_bridge` rooted at `.fantastic`. The `fantastic` CLI wires one on its first start: its seed writes a `store` agent (`file_bridge.tools`, `root: .fantastic`, `allow: ["."]`), so by default the tree and its records are saved under `.fantastic/`. Only when no such store exists do the records stay in memory, and the terminal then warns that nothing survives a restart. [State and durability](/fantastic/foundations/kernel/state/) covers that wiring.

#### reflect: the tree on demand

`reflect` is the discovery verb, and every agent answers it with the same core fields. The reply says what the agent is, not how to call it: its `id`, a one-line `sentence`, `parent_id`, `handler_module`, `display_name`, a `description` if the record has one, then the flat fields of the record. It also repeats the agent’s `can_call` and `callable_by`, so an agent can read its own reach without trying calls. Like any send, a reflect passes the [call gate](/fantastic/foundations/protocol/call-gate/) first.

On the root, `reflect` adds the fields that belong to the whole kernel: `runtime` (`rust` in the Rust kernel), `peers` (the kernels this one is connected to), `env` and `version`. The root’s loader adds more, such as the kernel’s `guid`.

#### The tree flag

By default a reflect carries the agent’s whole subtree under `tree`. That is fine for a first look and too much afterwards, so three flags shape it.

| flag | what the reply holds |
|---|---|
| `tree=all` (the default) | the nested subtree. Each node is `{id, sentence?, description?, mode?, task?, children}`, and a node’s `sentence` comes from the agent itself |
| `tree=ids` | a flat list of every id below, depth first, the agent first. It pages with `limit` and `after`, and `next` is the cursor |
| `detail=full` | with `tree=all`, a wiring node instead: `{id, parent_id, handler_module, display_name, description?, children}` plus the posture fields `ingress_rule`, `egress_rule`, `auth`, `root`, `allow`, `can_call` and `callable_by` where the record has them |
| `ignore_subtrees=[ids]` | each named branch becomes `{id, pruned: n}`, where n counts the agents the branch holds, itself included |
| `show_subtrees=[ids]` | only those branches, as a list. An id inside another shown id is covered by it. Show applies first, then ignore inside it |

A `tree` value other than `all` or `ids` leaves the tree out. The built-in manual writes that as `tree=none`. An id in `show_subtrees` or `ignore_subtrees` that is not in the reflected agent’s tree is refused with `bad_arg`, and the hint says that `tree=ids` lists the ids.

reflect with a pruned branch (illustrative id):

```
[{"target": "kernel", "payload": {"type": "reflect",
  "tree": "all", "ignore_subtrees": ["team"]}}]
```

*Animation: reflect: look without flooding* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/kernel/records/reflect.mp4). tree=ids returns every id below, depth first. ignore_subtrees=["team"] folds that branch to {id: "team", pruned: 3}. bundles=ids lists the kinds of agent that can be created. show_subtrees=["team"] answers with only the team branch.

#### The bundles flag

The kinds of agent that can be created are bundles, and `reflect` lists them on request. `bundles=ids` gives the names. `bundles=all` gives each one as `{name, handler_module}`, plus a `schema` when the bundle publishes one, so the fields a record of that kind takes can be read before any agent of it exists. The list also holds the folder bundles of this kernel’s root, and it pages with `limit` and `after`, with `bundles_next` as the cursor.

A scan that stays cheap is `tree=ids` with `bundles=ids`. A caller then reflects one id at a time, or uses `show_subtrees` and `ignore_subtrees` once it knows which part of the tree it works on. A reflect that is refused is never decorated with a tree.

Sources: README.md: everything is an agent (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/README.md#L16); the record and the agent (Rust) (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/rust/crates/fantastic-kernel/src/agent.rs#L52); create_agent and id minting (Rust) (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/rust/crates/fantastic-kernel/src/lifecycle.rs#L51); the record in Python (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/python/kernel/_agent.py#L632); reflect flags (Rust) (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/rust/crates/fantastic-kernel/src/reflect.rs#L300); show_subtrees and ignore_subtrees (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/rust/crates/fantastic-kernel/src/docs.rs#L271); the built-in reflect manual (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/rust/crates/bundles/fantastic-core/src/docs/reflect.md); the CLI’s first-start seed: the store agent (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/src/boot/seed.rs#L322); the Rust kernel crate (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/tree/main/src/lib/rust/crates/fantastic-kernel/src)

### Foundations › Kernel › Lifecycle

URL: https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/kernel/lifecycle/

An agent lives from the `create_agent` that makes its record to the `delete_agent` that removes it, and the kernel around it starts and stops. Each step is one kernel verb, and the Rust and Python runtimes do the same thing.

This page follows that order: create, update, delete, then the start sequence, the two stop verbs and what a restart reads back. The record that these verbs write is described in [Agents as records](/fantastic/foundations/kernel/records/).

#### Kernel verbs belong to the root

The kernel answers fourteen verbs: `create_agent`, `update_agent`, `delete_agent`, `list_agents`, `ps`, `cancel`, `ledger`, `ack_deadletter`, `await_set`, `await_cancel`, `kernel_start`, `shutdown_agents`, `kernel_stop` and `docs`. This page covers the lifecycle ones; [Tasks and waiting](/fantastic/foundations/kernel/tasks/) covers `ps`, `cancel` and the waits.

Only the root agent answers them. The agent a call names is the **operand**, not the actor: `create_agent` names the new agent’s parent, `delete_agent` the agent to remove. A kernel verb sent to any other agent is refused with `reason: "not_here"`, and the hint says to address `kernel` and to name the agent in `parent_id` or `id`.

They take the same [call gate](/fantastic/foundations/protocol/call-gate/) as any other send, against the root. Whoever holds a verb on the root holds it for every agent.

#### create_agent: placement is always stated

`create_agent` needs two arguments, `handler_module` and `parent_id`. There is no default parent: the call does not guess from who sent it. A missing `parent_id` is refused with `reason: "missing_arg"` and a hint to name the agent that will own the new one, “your own id for a tool you keep, or the root (‘kernel_state’) for a top-level agent”. The reserved name `kernel` also works for the root.

create a child of lead (illustrative ids):

```
[{"target": "kernel", "payload": {"type": "create_agent",
  "handler_module": "ram_store.tools", "parent_id": "lead"}}]
```

The `id` is optional. Without one, the kernel mints `<bundle>_<6 hex digits>` from the handler module’s second-to-last dotted segment, for example `ram_store_a3f9c1`. An id that is already in use is refused with `reason: "exists"`. Every other field in the payload becomes a flat field of the new record, its **meta**, and the keys the substrate owns (`root_path`, `ctx`, `parent`) are refused.

*Animation: create_agent: placement is stated* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/kernel/lifecycle/create.mp4). A create_agent with no parent_id is refused with missing_arg. With parent_id "lead" the child is registered under lead with a minted id, ram_store_a3f9c1, booted by the kernel before the reply, and the reply is its record. The ids are illustrative.

The kernel checks the meta before it creates anything: a grant map of the wrong shape, or a value the bundle’s own check rejects, is refused with `invalid_meta`. A `handler_module` that no installed bundle provides is not refused; the record is made and it answers no domain verbs until the bundle exists.

The new agent is registered under its parent, then booted at once. The kernel runs the child’s `boot` itself, as the child and without the call gate, before the reply. If the boot fails, the kernel prints the failure and the agent still exists. The reply is the new record, and the parent gets an `agent_created` message.

#### update_agent: a field is replaced, not merged

`update_agent` takes an `id` and any fields to set. Every field the call names is replaced, and a field it does not name is untouched. A dict field is therefore sent whole. The verb’s own doc puts it this way: “Granting one edge reads like a PATCH and behaves like a PUT.”

a map is replaced whole (illustrative):

```
before  can_call {"$self": "*", "a": ["reflect"]}
send    update_agent id=x can_call={"b": ["reflect"]}
after   can_call {"b": ["reflect"]}
```

To grant one more edge, restate every key to keep, including the baseline `$self`; the keys left out are gone. [Call gate and grants](/fantastic/foundations/protocol/call-gate/) explains the maps.

Some fields cannot be set. `handler_module` is fixed at create, because swapping it would leave a running agent whose state belongs to the old bundle. The substrate keys `root_path`, `ctx` and `parent` are refused too, and `parent_id` is ignored: where an agent sits comes from the tree, not from its meta. These checks run before the id is looked up.

The kernel checks grant maps and the bundle’s own rules for the new values, and refuses with `invalid_meta` when they fail. On success the reply is `updated: true`, the `id` and the new record, and the caller gets an `agent_updated` message that lists the changed field names. The root can be updated like any agent, which is how it gets its `memory_store_id` below.

#### delete_agent: the whole subtree, deepest first

`delete_agent` takes an `id` and removes that agent and everything below it. The root cannot be deleted: it owns persistence and answers the kernel verbs, so deleting it would leave no kernel. That is a `bad_arg` refusal.

Before it deletes anything, the kernel walks the subtree for `delete_lock`. If the target or any descendant carries `delete_lock: true`, the whole delete is refused with `reason: "locked"`. The refusal names the first blocker in `blocked_by`, and its hint is “clear the lock with update_agent, then delete again”. Nothing has changed at that point.

*Animation: delete_agent: the whole subtree* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/kernel/lifecycle/delete.mp4). delete_agent on team is refused because reviewer carries delete_lock. After update_agent clears it, the delete cascades deepest first, each agent running its on_delete hook, and the deleted ids are pruned from x’s can_call.

The cascade then runs per node, children first. For each agent the kernel runs the bundle’s `on_delete` hook, as that agent, then detaches the agent from its parent and drops it from the tree. A hook that raises is printed and the cascade goes on, so a delete cannot be blocked from inside.

- **Memory.** An AI agent’s `on_delete` removes its persisted rows from the memory store. `keep_memory: true` on the delete, the literal `true` only, keeps the rows of every agent in that subtree, for that one delete.
- **Grants.** After the cascade, every deleted id is removed from every other agent’s `can_call` and `callable_by`. An agent created later under the same id inherits no old edge.
- **Reply.** `deleted: true` and the `id`. The caller gets an `agent_deleted` message.

#### kernel_start: the order of boot

Loading a tree and booting it are two steps. The loader builds the agents from their records, and `kernel_start` runs the start sequence. The daemon runs the sequence once its tree is loaded, and it is also a verb an operator can send.

The sequence needs a **memory store**: the root’s `memory_store_id` must name an agent. The kernel keeps its execution rows there (the [ledger](/fantastic/foundations/protocol/ledger/), dead letters and named-call dedup), and there is no built-in default. Without one, the verb is refused with `reason: "missing_arg"` and `arg: "memory_store_id"`, and the hint is the fix:

the hint, verbatim:

```
create_agent parent_id=<root> handler_module=ram_store.tools id=memory
update_agent id=<root> memory_store_id=memory
```

*Animation: kernel_start: the order of boot* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/kernel/lifecycle/start.mp4). kernel_start on a root with no memory_store_id is refused. After update_agent names memory, the root boots (1), then memory (2), the kernel probes the store (3) and starts the flusher, then lead (4) and web (5) boot in registration order. The reply lists booted in that order.

1. Boot the root. Its boot gives the kernel a `guid` when the record has none.
2. Boot the memory store, before anyone who might call it.
3. Probe the store with a `read` as the operator. If it refuses the kernel, `kernel_start` refuses now, not on the first flush.
4. Write the reserved `next_id` bound to the root record, start the flusher that moves execution rows into the store, and restore the open `await_set` waits.
5. Boot every other agent in registration order, then complete the waits that are already due.

The reply is `started: true`, the `store` id and `booted`, the ids that booted in order. A second call is idempotent: it answers `started: true` and `already: true` with the store. If the root or the store fails to boot, `kernel_start` is refused. Any other agent that fails to boot is printed, and the sequence goes on. AI agents boot lazily: they read their own store on their first turn.

#### Stopping: shutdown_agents and kernel_stop

Two verbs stop things, and both are root-only. `shutdown_agents` stops the agents and leaves the process running. `kernel_stop` stops the whole process.

- **Drain.** `shutdown_agents` first refuses new work with `reason: "draining"`. A send made from inside work that is already live still passes.
- **Tell.** Every agent whose bundle declares a `shutdown` verb is sent `shutdown`, all at once, each with a 30-second bound. In the Python runtime an AI agent gets it as a message to persist what matters, and its tools still work.
- **Quiet.** The kernel waits up to 10 seconds for in-flight work. Whatever is left is cancelled through the normal `cancel` path, so `on_cancel` hooks run and subtrees die with their roots. Then it waits up to 2 seconds for each cancelled call to record its ending.

The reply is `drained: true`, `shut` (the ids told) and `cancelled`. The kernel keeps serving afterwards, so reads and `ledger` still work, until the process exits. A second call answers the same shape and shuts nothing new.

*Animation: shutdown_agents and kernel_stop* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/kernel/lifecycle/stop.mp4). shutdown_agents drains the kernel, sends shutdown to lead and web, and cancels task 7 that is still in flight. The reply lists shut and cancelled. kernel_stop then acknowledges, and about 100 ms later calls settle, the last rows flush, hooks run, the lock is released and the process exits 0. The ids are illustrative.

`kernel_stop` acknowledges first with `{"type": "kernel_stop", "ok": true}`. About 100 ms later, after the reply is on the wire, it asks the daemon to stop. The daemon then does the full teardown: drain, let every call settle (done, or cancelled into the dead letters), flush the last rows into the store, run each agent’s shutdown hook, release `.fantastic/lock.yaml` and exit 0. SIGINT and SIGTERM take the same path. Without a running serve loop, such as a one-shot CLI call, there is nothing to stop and the verb only acknowledges.

#### Restart is a new process

The kernel has no restart verb. A restart is `kernel_stop` followed by a new daemon, and the second start reads back what the first one persisted.

1. Take `.fantastic/lock.yaml`. One kernel runs per workdir; a lock whose holder died is taken over.
2. Read the root record from `.fantastic/agent.yaml` and every agent record under the children directory. A virgin workdir gets a fresh root.
3. Validate the records first. A bad id, a reserved key, a duplicate or an orphan refuses the boot. A record whose `handler_module` is not installed in this runtime is logged and skipped, together with its subtree.
4. Build the tree, then run `kernel_start` as above. With no `memory_store_id` on the root, the daemon tears down, releases the lock and exits with an error.

Records come back when the root writes them to disk as agents are created and updated, which it does only through a `file_bridge` rooted at `.fantastic`. The memory store is a separate matter: a `ram_store`, as in the example above, holds its rows in RAM and loses them with the process. What a store keeps across a restart is the subject of [State and durability](/fantastic/foundations/kernel/state/).

The headless Rust daemon starts only when the tree contains a `web.tools` agent. With nothing to serve, it exits quietly with code 0 and takes no lock.

Sources: kernel_verbs.rs: the fourteen verbs, their docs, shutdown_agents and kernel_stop (Rust) (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/rust/crates/fantastic-kernel/src/send/kernel_verbs.rs#L14); lifecycle.rs: create_agent, delete_agent, the cascade and grant pruning (Rust) (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/rust/crates/fantastic-kernel/src/lifecycle.rs#L127); executions.rs: Kernel::start, the start sequence (Rust) (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/rust/crates/fantastic-kernel/src/executions.rs#L193); kernel.rs: shutdown_agents and the graceful shutdown (Rust) (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/rust/crates/fantastic-kernel/src/kernel.rs#L488); bootstrap.rs: lock, read the tree, build it (Rust) (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/rust/crates/fantastic-kernel/src/bootstrap.rs#L1); _agent.py: the Python kernel verbs, delete and cascade (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/python/kernel/_agent.py#L2695); _kernel.py: the Python start and shutdown_agents (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/python/kernel/_kernel.py#L662); main.rs: the daemon, start to exit (Rust) (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/rust/crates/fantastic-cli/src/main.rs#L608)

### Foundations › Kernel › Bundles and twin runtimes

URL: https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/kernel/bundles/

An agent is a record, and its record names a `handler_module`. The **bundle** behind that name is the code that answers the agent’s own verbs. Every kernel keeps its bundles in a catalog and resolves the name against it.

Fantastic ships kernels in more than one language. This page compares the Rust and the Python kernels; a TypeScript kernel also exists and reports runtime `"ts"`. The Rust and Python kernels fill that catalog differently, but a caller sends the same messages to either (see [Messages and verbs](/fantastic/foundations/protocol/messages/) and [Call gate and grants](/fantastic/foundations/protocol/call-gate/)).

#### One bundle per handler module

A send to an agent first meets the **kernel verbs**: `create_agent`, `delete_agent`, `update_agent`, `list_agents`, `ps`, `cancel`, `ledger`, `ack_deadletter`, `kernel_start`, `shutdown_agents`, `kernel_stop`, `await_set`, `await_cancel` and `docs`. The kernel answers these itself, at the root. They are the same fourteen in Rust and in Python.

Any other verb goes to the agent’s bundle. In Python the kernel calls `handler(id, payload, agent)` in the module that `handler_module` names. In Rust the registry returns the `Bundle` that is registered under that string, and the kernel calls its `handle`.

one name, two ways in:

```
file_bridge.tools        # a handler_module, as stored in an agent's record
handler(id, payload, agent)   # Python: the callable in that module
Bundle::handle(...)           # Rust: the method of the registered bundle
```

A bundle can also hook the agent’s life: Rust’s `Bundle` has `on_delete`, `on_cancel` and `on_shutdown`, each a no-op by default.

#### Rust: linked at build time

A Rust bundle is a crate that implements the `Bundle` trait. The file that defines the trait states it plainly: “Bundles aren’t dynamically loaded — every Rust bundle is a crate linked into the binary at compile time.”

The `fantastic` binary builds a `BundleRegistry` in `register_default_bundles()` and calls `register("file_bridge.tools", …)` for each bundle it ships. To add a bundle to a build, add its crate to the workspace and register it there. The `exec_bridge` and `py_agent` bundles register only when the `full` feature is on, and the CLI builds with `full` by default.

A `create_agent` that names an unregistered bundle still makes the record ([Lifecycle](/fantastic/foundations/kernel/lifecycle/)). A domain verb sent to that agent is refused as `unhandled`, with Python’s own text, `No module named 'absent_bundle'` for the handler module `absent_bundle.tools`. A caller sees one message from both kernels.

*Animation: From handler_module to code* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/kernel/bundles/resolve.mp4). A send reaches an agent whose record says handler_module file_bridge.tools. In the Rust kernel the registry holds a crate linked at build time under that string. In the Python kernel the fantastic.bundles entry-point catalog names the module. Both reach the bundle. A name absent_bundle.tools is in neither, and both answer No module named absent_bundle.

#### Python: found by entry point

A Python bundle is “anything with a `handler(id, payload, agent)` callable” in its module. A package publishes it in the `fantastic.bundles` entry-point group, for example `file_bridge = "file_bridge.tools"`.

The kernel resolves a `handler_module` only from that catalog. It never imports an arbitrary name from `sys.path`, so a `create_agent` cannot make the kernel run a module that no package published. A name outside the catalog fails as `No module named '<package>'`.

The catalog is read live. A name the kernel has not seen re-scans the entry points once, so a bundle installed while the kernel runs resolves on its first lookup. Test and probe modules that have no entry point register through `register_unlisted`: they dispatch, but never appear in the catalog.

Both kernels list their bundles in `reflect bundles=all`: the entry points in Python, the installed registry entries in Rust. Unlisted test bundles stay out of it.

#### Folder bundles: a new kind of agent without a rebuild

A **folder bundle** is a folder `bundles/<name>/` inside a kernel’s root (`.fantastic/`) that holds a `bundle.yaml`. It extends a bundled agent named by `base`. On main the one base a folder can extend is `py_agent`. The folder’s name becomes the `handler_module` of its instances.

Both runtimes load folder bundles, with the same rules. A folder bundle needs no entry point in Python and no new crate in Rust. The `py_agent` base it extends is itself a bundle: a registered crate in Rust (under `full`) and a bundled module in Python.

bundles/notes/bundle.yaml (illustrative):

```
base: py_agent
sentence: Keeps short notes.
command: [python3, agent.py]
verbs:
  add: "args: text:str (req). Returns {id}."
```

Folders are read at boot, before the agent tree loads, so an instance’s handler resolves. A folder that fails any check is listed in `reflect bundles=all` with an `error` and is never loaded. The checks are, in order:

1. The folder name uses letters, digits, `_` and `-`, and starts with a letter or `_`.
2. The name is not a built-in bundle’s name: “a folder may not shadow it.”
3. `bundle.yaml` exists, parses, and is a mapping.
4. `base` is present: the bundled agent it extends.
5. `sentence` is present: one line saying what the bundle is.
6. `base` names a bundled agent that a folder can extend.
7. The base accepts the rest: for `py_agent`, a `command` (the program’s argv, run with the folder as its working directory) and a `verbs` map from verb to doc. `reflect`, `boot` and `shutdown` are reserved.

*Animation: A folder bundle loads at boot* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/kernel/bundles/folder.mp4). At boot the kernel reads bundles/notes/bundle.yaml. It checks the folder name, that notes is not a built-in bundle, and that base py_agent and a sentence are present; the bundle registers. create_agent with handler_module notes makes an instance. The kernel starts the program, which says hello with its verbs, and the verbs match bundle.yaml.

Each instance, made with `create_agent handler_module=notes`, is a full agent. The kernel starts the program when the instance boots and kills it when the instance is deleted or the kernel stops. The program first says `{"op": "hello", "verbs": [...]}`; those verbs must equal the `verbs` in `bundle.yaml`, or the instance stops and says why. After that the kernel sends it `{"op": "call", ...}` and the program answers `{"op": "result", ...}`.

Nothing respawns a program that exits. `reload_bundle {name}`, a root verb, re-reads the folder and restarts every live instance of it. If the new `bundle.yaml` no longer loads, the call is refused and the live instances keep the previous load.

The program runs with the user’s OS rights. Its own subprocesses, files and network do not pass the call gate; only the verbs that reach it do.

#### Twin runtimes: same verbs, different loading

The Rust and Python kernels answer the same fourteen kernel verbs, and Rust’s verb docs are written to mirror Python’s. A client that talks to one can talk to the other. The root `reflect` reports which one it reached in its `runtime` field; the TypeScript kernel reports `"ts"` there and is not covered on this page.

|  | Rust | Python |
|---|---|---|
| built-in bundles reach the kernel | crates linked at compile time, registered in `register_default_bundles()` | entry points in the `fantastic.bundles` group |
| a bundle is | a `Bundle` trait implementation | a module with `handler(id, payload, agent)` |
| an unknown handler module | `No module named '…'` | `No module named '…'` |
| folder bundles (`base: py_agent`) | yes | yes |
| kernel verbs | the same 14 | the same 14 |
| root `reflect` reports `runtime` | `"rust"` | `"python"` |

*Animation: Rust and Python, one set of verbs* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/kernel/bundles/twin.mp4). The same reflect is sent to a Rust kernel and a Python kernel. The root reflect reports a runtime field with the same field names and order in both, and only its value differs: rust in one and python in the other. This clip shows the Rust and Python kernels; a TypeScript kernel also exists. Below them sit the same fourteen kernel verbs.

Sources: Rust: the Bundle trait and registry (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/rust/crates/fantastic-kernel/src/bundle.rs#L1); Rust: register_default_bundles() (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/rust/crates/fantastic-cli/src/main.rs#L45); Python: bundle discovery (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/python/kernel/_bundles.py#L1); Python: the system verbs (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/python/kernel/_agent.py#L129); Rust: folder bundle loader (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/rust/crates/bundles/fantastic-core/src/folders.rs#L31); Python: folder bundle loader (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/python/bundled_agents/loader/kernel_state/src/kernel_state/tools.py#L123); py_agent, the folder base (Python) (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/python/bundled_agents/io/py_agent/src/py_agent/tools.py#L1); py_agent, the folder base (Rust) (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/tree/main/src/lib/rust/crates/bundles/fantastic-py-agent)

### Foundations › Kernel › Tasks and waiting

URL: https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/kernel/tasks/

Every send that is running right now is a **task**. The kernel keeps them in one table, so any caller with the grant can list work in flight, stop it, or wait for a group of agents to finish.

This page covers the task table and `ps`, `cancel` of a task and everything below it, and `await_set`, which wakes a lead once for a whole set of reports. The Rust and Python runtimes implement the same behaviour. How a send is checked first is on [Call gate and grants](/fantastic/foundations/protocol/call-gate/).

#### The task table and ps

A task is one in-flight dispatch, not an agent. When a send reaches its target, the kernel adds a row to the **task table** for it and removes the row when the dispatch ends. The row is made before the handler runs, so a task can be stopped from its first moment.

Tasks form a tree. A send made inside a handler is a child of that handler’s task. A send made outside every dispatch, such as one from the CLI or a test, has no parent and is a root, “like a process spawned by init.” Work that a bundle forks out of a dispatch, such as an exec job’s output pump, is registered as a task too, so it also shows up in the table and can be cancelled.

A task id is a plain integer from the kernel’s one id counter. It is the same number that an outcome carries as its `pid`, so the id in `ps` is the id you give `cancel`. ([Messages and verbs](/fantastic/foundations/protocol/messages/) covers outcomes.)

`ps` answers with the whole table, kernel-wide, oldest row first, unless you page it. Each row has five fields:

ps (shape, illustrative values):

```
{"tasks": [{"id": 42, "agent": "planner", "parent": 41,
            "verb": "run", "started_at": 1790000000.5}],
 "next": null}
```

| field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `id` | the task’s number |
| `agent` | the agent that is handling the dispatch |
| `parent` | the task that made this send, or `null` for a root |
| `verb` | the verb being handled |
| `started_at` | seconds since the epoch |

*Animation: ps: the task table* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/kernel/tasks/ps.mp4). Five tasks run: 41 lead, its children 42 planner and 45 notes, and below 42 the tasks 43 exec_bridge and 44 model. The operator sends ps to kernel. The reply lists one row per task, oldest first, with id, agent, parent and verb. The last row, 46, is the ps dispatch itself. The parent column ties each row back to its place in the tree. Ids, agents and verbs are illustrative.

`ps` lists its own row, because it is a dispatch like any other. A reply can be paged: `limit` and an `after` cursor work as in `list_agents`, and `next` is `null` when no further page exists. The table is live, so a row that finishes while you page may be missed.

When a task ends, its surviving children move up to its parent. Work that outlives the dispatch that started it therefore stays inside its caller’s subtree, where `cancel` on the caller still reaches it.

`ps` and `cancel` are kernel verbs: the root answers them, so they are sent to `kernel`. They pass the same call gate as any other verb. An agent that holds the grant can read `ps` and cancel another agent’s runaway work.

#### cancel: a task and its subtree

`cancel {task_id}` kills that task and every task below it, children first, “like a process group.” The id may be an integer, its decimal string, or the name the caller gave its own execution. It answers with the ids it killed:

cancel (illustrative ids):

```
[{"target": "kernel", "payload": {"type": "cancel", "task_id": 42}}]
→ {"cancelled": true, "killed": [43, 44, 42]}
```

An unknown or finished id is not an error. The answer is `{"cancelled": false, "killed": []}`. A missing `task_id` is refused with the usual shape ([Refusals](/fantastic/foundations/protocol/refusals/)).

#### Two phases

Dropping a task frees no operating-system resource: a child process or a socket stays open. So `cancel` runs in two phases, named after SIGTERM and SIGKILL.

1. **Hooks.** The kernel marks every task in the subtree as dying. It then awaits each agent’s bundle `on_cancel` hook, with all tasks still alive, so no handler sees a half-killed group. A hook runs as its own agent. If a hook fails, the error is logged and the kill goes on: cancel cannot be refused by a bundle.
2. **Abort.** The kernel stops the tasks leaves first, with no wait in between, so a parent cannot resume between its child’s death and its own.

*Animation: cancel: a task and its subtree* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/kernel/tasks/cancel.mp4). cancel on task 42 first runs every on_cancel hook in its subtree while the tasks are alive: a child process is killed and a generation is closed. Then the tasks abort, leaves first. The sibling 45 and the parent 41 keep running. cancel answers cancelled true with the killed ids, and the waiting send settles as cancelled.

The hooks are where real resources go. An `exec_bridge` job’s `on_cancel` kills the job’s child process. An AI backend’s `on_cancel` closes the stopped turn: its open parts abort and its status goes to `done` with reason `cancelled`.

The caller that was waiting on the cancelled send is not killed. Its item settles with status `cancelled` and the reply `{"cancelled": true}`. Nothing raises out of `send`. A caller that is itself inside the dying subtree does not resume either. It waits for its own stop.

Two cases go the same way as `cancel`. A send with its own `timeout` kills its task through the same front door, so hooks run first, and its item settles as `timed_out`. And the kernel’s own service tasks, such as the loop that flushes the ledger to the memory store, refuse `cancel` with a `bad_arg` refusal. They stay listed in `ps` until the kernel stops. See [Ledger and dead letters](/fantastic/foundations/protocol/ledger/) for what a cancelled item leaves behind.

#### await_set: one wake for a set

A lead that waits for several workers would otherwise wake on every report and send its whole context again each time. `await_set {ids, timeout_s?, label?}` replaces that with one wake. It is a kernel verb, sent to `kernel` by the agent that wants to wait, and it answers at once:

await_set (illustrative ids):

```
[{"target": "kernel", "payload": {"type": "await_set",
  "ids": ["w1", "w2", "w3"], "timeout_s": 60}}]
→ {"wait_id": 50, "label": null, "ids": ["w1", "w2", "w3"], "timeout_s": 60}
```

The `wait_id` is another number from the kernel’s id counter. `label` is an optional string that comes back in the final message. The verb refuses an operator send, since nobody could be woken. It also refuses a missing or empty `ids`, an id that names no agent, the caller’s own id, a `timeout_s` that is not a positive number, and a `label` that is not a string.

The signal each worker sends is a plain message, `{"type": "report", "state": ..., "result": ...}`, sent to the lead. No `report` verb is involved. While the wait is open, a report from a named agent is held instead of delivered, and the reporter is answered at once with `{"held": true, "wait_id": 50}`, so it never blocks on the lead. A second report from the same agent replaces its first.

*Animation: await_set: one wake for a set* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/kernel/tasks/await.mp4). A lead sends await_set for w1, w2 and w3 with a timeout of 60 seconds and gets wait_id 50 back at once. Each worker then sends a report. The kernel holds each one and answers the worker held, and the count at the lead goes from 0 to 3 of 3. With all three in, the lead receives one message with wait_id 50, a done entry per worker, an empty missing list and timed_out false. Ids are illustrative.

When every named agent has reported, or `timeout_s` passes, the lead receives one message:

the one message:

```
{"type": "send", "text": "<the same body as compact JSON>",
 "wait_id": 50, "label": null,
 "done": [{"id": "w1", "state": ..., "result": ...}, ...],
 "missing": [], "timed_out": false}
```

`done` follows the order of `ids`, and `text` is the body as compact JSON, for a model to read. After a timeout, `done` holds the agents that reported, `missing` names the rest and `timed_out` is `true`. The last report and the timer cannot both win: the kernel claims the wait once, so the lead is woken once.

`await_cancel {wait_id}` drops the caller’s own wait. The reports it held are then delivered one by one, each as its own message from the agent that sent it, in the order they were held. The answer is `{"cancelled": true, "wait_id": 50, "released": 2}`. A wait that is unknown, or belongs to another agent, answers `{"cancelled": false, "wait_id": ..., "released": 0}`.

A wait is stored as rows in the kernel’s memory store, so it survives a restart: on start the kernel rebuilds each open wait, completes the ones already due, and re-arms the timers of the rest. A kernel that is stopping delivers nothing and leaves the wait open for the next start. If the lead has left the tree, nobody is woken.

Sources: tasks.rs: the task table, ps rows and cancel (Rust) (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/rust/crates/fantastic-kernel/src/tasks.rs#L1); kernel_verbs.rs: ps, cancel and the kernel verb docs (Rust) (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/rust/crates/fantastic-kernel/src/send/kernel_verbs.rs#L14); _kernel.py: task_rows and cancel_task (Python) (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/python/kernel/_kernel.py#L1235); await_set.rs: held reports, the one message, restore (Rust) (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/rust/crates/fantastic-kernel/src/await_set.rs#L1); _await.py: await_set (Python) (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/python/kernel/_await.py#L1); exec_bridge on_cancel: SIGKILL of a job (Rust) (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/rust/crates/bundles/fantastic-exec-bridge/src/lib.rs#L606); ai_core on_cancel: closing a stopped turn (Rust) (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/rust/crates/bundles/fantastic-ai-core/src/verbs.rs#L229)

### Foundations › Kernel › State and durability

URL: https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/kernel/state/

Two different things can survive a restart. The **tree** is the agents and their records. The **rows** are the kernel’s execution rows and each AI agent’s conversation. They live in different places and persist through different agents, so a kernel can keep one and lose the other.

This page covers the `kernel_state` root that owns the tree, the single id counter that names everything, and what a restart and a crash leave behind. The ledger and dead letters are on [their own page](/fantastic/foundations/protocol/ledger/).

#### The kernel_state root

The root of every tree is an agent with the id `kernel_state` and the handler module `kernel_state.tools`. It owns the `.fantastic/` directory: it turns records into `agent.yaml` files, maps the tree to paths and writes changes. The reserved address `kernel` always names this root, whatever its id.

A new directory has no root record. The bootstrap seeds one, `{id: kernel_state, handler_module: kernel_state.tools}`, and writes it to `.fantastic/agent.yaml` when the first mode takes the directory lock. A root `agent.yaml` that exists but does not parse is never written over: the boot stops and asks you to fix or remove it.

#### The tree needs a file_bridge

The root does not write the children of the tree by itself. It writes them only through a **provider** that it discovers: a `file_bridge` agent anywhere below the root whose `root` resolves to `.fantastic`. If several match, the shallowest wins. Each change is written 150 ms after it happens, to a temporary file that is then renamed over `agent.yaml`.

With no provider, nothing is written. The tree lives in RAM and is lost on restart, and there is no direct-write fallback. A provider that refuses, for example because its `allow` list does not cover the records, fails loudly: the refusal goes to stderr and the root’s `reflect` shows it.

root reflect: wired, or RAM (illustrative id):

```
{"persistence": {"provider": "store"}}
{"persistence": {"provider": null}}
```

On a graceful stop, the root writes its last pending records before the agents are torn down, while the provider is still alive. The stop never deletes records, so the next boot rehydrates the tree. A record whose bundle this runtime does not have is skipped with one line on stderr, together with its subtree. The record stays on disk, and a build that has the bundle loads it later.

#### The guid

The root also mints the kernel’s instance `guid` once, at boot, and keeps it in the root record. With a provider, later boots read it back unchanged. Without one, the guid exists only in memory, and the next boot mints a new one.

#### One counter names everything

A call, a forked task, a settle row, a wait and an AI agent’s conversation row all take their id from one **counter**, a 64-bit integer that starts at 1. The same number is what `ps` lists, what `cancel` takes, what a reply is tagged with and what a store row is keyed by.

The counter is kernel-wide and only goes up. If id `a` is smaller than id `b`, `a` was created first, across all agents. An id is never reused, so a stale `cancel` on an old id kills nothing.

*Animation: One counter names everything* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/kernel/state/ids.mp4). A call takes id 41, a forked task 42 and its settle row 43, all from the same counter. Each id is larger than the one before, across agents, and none is reused. The root record holds only the reserved bound, next_id: 1001.

#### Reserved in blocks of 1000

The kernel reserves ids in blocks of 1000 and keeps only the upper bound, `next_id`, in the root record next to `guid`.

1. A load resumes at the root record’s `next_id`, never lower, and reserves its first block in memory. A load writes nothing.
2. `kernel_start` writes that bound into the root record.
3. When a started kernel mints an id at or past the bound, it reserves the next 1000 and writes the new bound.

the root record (illustrative):

```
next_id: 1001     # ids up to 1000 may have been handed out
next_id: 2001     # written when id 1001 is minted
```

So a restart begins at the stored bound, and ids below it are not issued again. The bound reaches disk through the same debounced write (150 ms) as any other record change. After a crash, up to one block of ids is skipped. The gaps are harmless because ids are opaque.

*Animation: Ids reserved in blocks* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/kernel/state/reserve.mp4). The root record holds next_id: 1001. When the kernel mints id 1001 it reserves the next block and writes next_id: 2001. The process crashes after id 1500. On restart the counter resumes at 2001, so ids 1501 to 2000 are skipped and none is issued twice.

The guid and the counter persist together. A root that is not durable mints a new guid on its next boot. Every store key starts with the guid, so the new keys cannot collide with the ids that restart from 1. The one case the kernel cannot defend is an old `agent.yaml` restored under the same guid, which moves the counter backwards. That is for the administrator to prevent.

#### Rows live in a memory store

The kernel keeps no conversation and no message log in the tree. Its execution rows (`call`, `settle`, `task`, `ack`, and the rows of an `await_set` wait) are minted in RAM and flushed, 150 ms after a change, into the **memory store** that the root record names in `memory_store_id`. Each AI agent names its own store for its turns, folds and views.

`kernel_start` refuses when the root names no store, and there is no default. The start sequence, step by step on [Lifecycle](/fantastic/foundations/kernel/lifecycle/), boots the root first, which supplies the guid, then the store, which is probed to confirm that it serves the operator. Then it writes the id bound, starts the flusher, rebuilds the open waits, and boots every other agent in registration order.

Every row in a store is keyed `<kernel guid>|<agent id>`, and `<guid>|kernel` is the operator and the kernel’s own bookkeeping. Two stores ship with the kernel, and they answer the same verbs ([Memory stores](/fantastic/foundations/agents/memory-stores/)):

| store | durable | after a restart |
|---|---|---|
| `ram_store` | no | empty: everything it holds ends with the process |
| `sqlite_store` | yes | one SQLite file; the rows are read back |

The same store holds the data that gives a restart its meaning: the ledger, dead letters, named-call dedup and every AI agent’s memory. A reply’s body is not stored, only a one-line `origin` that says what to re-read.

The ledger is trimmed once it passes `ledger_cap` (1,000,000 rows by default in Python), oldest settled executions first, unnamed before named. A dead letter that nobody has acknowledged is kept ([Ledger and dead letters](/fantastic/foundations/protocol/ledger/)).

#### What survives a restart

The answer depends on which two agents you wired, a `file_bridge` rooted at `.fantastic` and a memory store.

The `fantastic` CLI wires the first one for you. Its first-start seed writes a `store` agent, a `file_bridge` (`file_bridge.tools`) with `root: .fantastic` and `allow: ["."]`, so by default the tree and its records are saved under `.fantastic/`. The terminal’s `volatile()` check is true only when no such store exists, and then the statusline warns: “no store wired — rows will not survive a restart.”

| what | survives when | otherwise |
|---|---|---|
| The agent tree, and bundle sidecars such as a scheduler’s schedules | a `file_bridge` is rooted at `.fantastic` | gone; only the seeded root record is on disk |
| The kernel’s `guid` and the id counter | the root record is persisted, which also needs that `file_bridge` | a new guid, and ids restart from 1 |
| Settled named executions, dead letters and acknowledgements | the memory store is durable, like `sqlite_store` | gone with the process |
| Open `await_set` waits | the memory store is durable | gone with the process |
| An AI agent’s conversation | its memory store is durable | gone with the process |

*Animation: What survives a restart* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/kernel/state/restart.mp4). Before the restart, the kernel has an agent tree on disk through a file_bridge, a ram_store and a sqlite_store. After the restart the tree is back and so are the rows in sqlite_store. The rows in ram_store are gone.

A durable store alone is not enough. Its rows are keyed by the guid, so a kernel with a `sqlite_store` but no `file_bridge` gets a new guid on every boot and never finds its old rows. Wire both.

#### Two limits

A call that is in flight when the process dies has no settle row. Re-sending it runs it again, unless the send gave it a name that already settled. On a graceful stop, the drain settles interrupted calls as `cancelled`, which makes them dead letters. Replaying an interrupted turn to where it stopped is not built.

Keep the records store and your data apart. The `file_bridge` that persists records can rewrite any record, including its own grants, so grant it as narrowly as you can: the CLI’s seed lists only `user` in its `callable_by`. The files your agents read and write go through a second `file_bridge`, which the seed also writes: `files`, rooted at the project folder.

Sources: kernel_state/tools.py: provider discovery, flush loop, guid (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/python/bundled_agents/loader/kernel_state/src/kernel_state/tools.py#L329); persistence.md: durable state, memory stores, the counter (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/python/bundled_agents/loader/kernel_state/src/kernel_state/docs/persistence.md#L5); _kernel.py: the counter, kernel_start, load (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/python/kernel/_kernel.py#L485); rows.rs: the counter in the Rust kernel (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/rust/crates/fantastic-kernel/src/rows.rs#L11); persistence.rs: find_store_for and the record writer (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/rust/crates/fantastic-kernel/src/persistence.rs#L163); seed.rs: the CLI’s first-start seed and its store agent (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/src/boot/seed.rs#L322); blueprint.yaml: the seeded store and files agents (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/blueprint.yaml#L79); host.rs: volatile() (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/src/kern/host.rs#L622); sqlite_store readme (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/python/bundled_agents/memory/sqlite_store/src/sqlite_store/readme.md); ram_store readme (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/python/bundled_agents/memory/ram_store/src/ram_store/readme.md)

### Foundations › Agents

URL: https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/agents/

Everything in Fantastic is an agent, so what it can do is the set of agents it ships. Each is a bundle that answers its own verbs behind the same call gate.

#### What ships

- **AI agents** over vLLM, Ollama, the OpenAI Responses API and Anthropic’s Messages API, plus Apple’s on-device model on macOS. Tool calling is Fantastic’s own prompt-taught `<call>` grammar, not a provider tool API, so any capable model drives the same verbs. [AI agent](/fantastic/foundations/agents/ai-agent/) follows one turn, and [Model backends](/fantastic/foundations/agents/ai-agent/backends/) the five providers.
- **Memory**: every message lives in a [memory store](/fantastic/foundations/agents/memory-stores/) agent. AI agents fold, recall and page their own history.
- **IO legs**: `file_bridge` for files, edits, streams and watches; `exec_bridge` for allow-listed commands and terminals; `web_ws` and `web_rest` for the browser and HTTP; `ws_bridge` from one kernel to another; `mcp_client` for a remote MCP server’s tools as verbs.
- **Kernel services**: a scheduler, and [credentials by reference](/fantastic/foundations/agents/credential-store/), with keys bound to one host.

The AI agent keeps a long conversation in a finite window by folding it: a finished stretch of work becomes one appended row that names what it hides.

*Animation: A fold is a new row* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/agents/ai-agent/context-folding/fold.mp4). context_fold over rows 3 to 8 appends one fold row (13) to the store, with refs to its members; nothing is deleted. In the view the fold sits at its anchor, row 3, in place of its members, and everything before the range keeps its exact bytes.

### Foundations › Agents › AI agent

URL: https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/agents/ai-agent/

An **AI agent** is an ordinary agent whose handler talks to a language model. It is the shared crate `ai_core`, in Rust and in Python, behind a small interface called a provider. A backend such as ollama, vllm, responses or anthropic supplies only that provider.

This page follows what happens when a message reaches an AI agent: the prompt it builds, the one pass it runs, the calls the model writes, the chain that continues from their replies, the rows it leaves behind, and the verbs that pause it. Three parts have their own pages: [Context folding](/fantastic/foundations/agents/ai-agent/context-folding/), [Forking and marks](/fantastic/foundations/agents/ai-agent/forking/) and [Model backends](/fantastic/foundations/agents/ai-agent/backends/).

#### One pass behind a provider seam

Each `send` to an AI agent runs exactly one **pass**: it assembles the prompt, fits it to the context window, streams the model’s tokens, and appends the turn to the agent’s history. The code says so itself: “ONE provider pass per `send`.”

The **provider** is the only part that knows a vendor. It takes plain chat messages (a role and text) and yields text tokens. It does no tool calling, holds no agent state, and never uses a vendor’s native tool interface. Its one protocol duty is the reasoning channel: it wraps a reasoning model’s deliberation in `<think>` and `</think>` once per turn, so a turn that is all thinking is not read as empty.

- `chat(messages, max_tokens)` streams the completion as tokens.
- `model()` names the upstream model.
- `ready()` can refuse the turn up front, before anything is assembled.
- `report()` returns what the endpoint reported about the pass, such as its own prompt-token count.

A pass runs its steps in a fixed order: the provider’s `ready()` check, the caching-mode check, any recall owed from the last fold, prompt assembly, context projection, and only then `chat`. A failure at any step ends the turn with a reason instead of a half answer. The two runtimes agree on this contract; the Rust crate is a port of the Python `ai_core`, which its comments call canonical.

*Animation: One pass: rows and a prompt in, a stream out* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/agents/ai-agent/pass.mp4). A send reaches the AI agent. The system block (tree, self, how-to) and the rows from its memory store go to the provider. Tokens stream back. The agent appends two rows, the incoming message and the answer.

#### The prompt is built from the live tree

The default system block is three parts joined by blank lines: `{tree}`, `{self}` and `{howto}`. `{tree}` is the kernel’s primer, a flat list of agent ids and the bundle names. `{self}` is the agent’s own identity: its `id`, `description`, `memory_store_id`, `can_call` and `callable_by`. `{howto}` is fixed text that teaches the call envelope, grants, replies and the context window.

Nothing in the block lists other agents’ verbs. To learn what a target answers, the model sends `kernel` a `docs` with `<of>` naming the agent. That reply is transient: after the model’s next message it shrinks to a one-line stub.

The block states the mechanism and no strategy. The source comment is explicit that the default prompt says nothing about looping, orienting, iterating or finishing, and a test pins it. A record can replace the block with its own `system_prompt`, or a file named by `system_prompt_file`; a `send` can replace it for one delivery. The first of those that is set wins, and the placeholders above are filled in whichever block is used. `pre_system_prompt` and `post_system_prompt` on the record wrap it without replacing anything.

Everything after the block is the conversation: the rows in the agent’s store, shaped to a view that fits the window ([Context folding](/fantastic/foundations/agents/ai-agent/context-folding/)).

#### Tools are verbs, written as text

A model calls an agent by writing a `<call>` element in its answer: one child tag per argument, no JSON, no escaping. `<target_id>` names the agent, `<type>` is the verb, and every other child is an argument. This is the only envelope the parser reads.

a call (illustrative ids):

```
<call name="send">
<target_id>notes</target_id>
<type>read</type>
<path>todo.md</path>
</call>
```

It is the same `{target, payload}` item that [every message](/fantastic/foundations/protocol/messages/) carries, written as text. So an AI agent has no tool list of its own: its tools are the verbs of every agent it may reach. Four call names parse: `send`, `done`, `await` and `inquiry_answer`. The last three are control calls, not dispatches.

The calls run as the agent, so the [call gate](/fantastic/foundations/protocol/call-gate/) decides each one. The prompt tells the model to read its `can_call` before the first call, because a call outside it is refused and costs a turn.

Only the answer acts. A `<call>` written inside thinking never runs, and thinking is stripped before the turn is stored. A pass that stops with a call still open dispatches nothing at all, even its closed calls, and leaves a marker row in place of a half answer.

#### The loop is a chain of passes

No code loops inside a pass. The loop is a **chain**: after a pass, the router dispatches every call the model wrote in one batch, and the calls run concurrently. Everything owed to one destination comes back as one message, one block per call, each headed by its pid:

a reply batch, abridged (illustrative pids and batch token):

```
[reply to 1042 · notes read · 1 of 2 in batch b7]
…
[reply to 1043 · notes list · 2 of 2 in batch b7]
…
```

The model never sees half a batch. `reply_to` decides where a reply goes: back to the caller by default, another agent’s id, or `null` to discard it. When the batch lands on the agent itself, that is the next pass, and the chain goes on when a reply batch lands on the agent, or when the router sends a reminder (below).

*Animation: A chain is passes joined by replies* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/agents/ai-agent/chain.mp4). Pass 1 writes two calls. They run concurrently and come back as one reply batch addressed to the agent. That starts pass 2, which writes done, and the chain ends.

#### How a chain ends

- `done` ends it explicitly. Nothing runs and nothing reminds.
- `await` stops until something lands. Status ends with `reason: awaiting` and the `pending` count. With nothing in flight it ends the chain and stores a note, `nothing_to_await`.
- A turn with no calls dispatched ends it only after the reminders run out (below).

A turn that dispatches no call at all is not the end. The router stores a reminder, `[no call was dispatched]`, and the agent runs again. A turn that was only thinking has its answer discarded and never stored (the incoming row stays), and gets an extra line saying so. The second silent turn in a row escalates the reminder.

Ten silent turns in a row end the chain with status `done`, `reason: gave_up`. The record field `misfire_limit` replaces the ten. Any call resets the count, `done` and `await` included.

*Animation: A turn with no call is reminded* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/agents/ai-agent/nudge.mp4). The agent answers with prose and no call. The router stores a reminder and the agent runs again. Ten silent turns in a row end the chain with gave_up; a done call ends it at once.

`cancel` ends a runaway chain like any other task ([Tasks and waiting](/fantastic/foundations/kernel/tasks/)).

#### History is rows in a store

The conversation is never kept in the agent. It lives in the **memory store** the record names with `memory_store_id`, one row per message, under the agent’s own key. A turn adds two rows: the incoming message, `{role: "user", content, id, parent}`, and the answer, `{role: "assistant", content, id, parent}` with the thinking removed.

Row ids come from the kernel’s counter ([State and durability](/fantastic/foundations/kernel/state/)), minted at the moment of the append. An id therefore orders rows in time, and after a restart the conversation comes back in the order it was lived. When the incoming message is a reply batch, its `parent` is the turn named by the `↑N` on its first tag.

Writes go to the store first and into the agent’s in-memory head only when the store took them. The head is the rows since the last `clear`, read once on the first turn after boot. No store named means the agent fails loud at boot and on its first turn; nothing falls back to RAM. A store that refuses mid-turn fails the turn.
